newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria summit pushes to liberalise economy.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria summit pushes to liberalise economy.

text.p: Liberalise more quickly or stagnate further was the message to emerge from a summit on Nigeria's economy on Thursday.
Hundreds of businessmen and officials of the military government gathered in the capital Abuja in the search for policies to reform the economy and achieve long term growth.
While there was emphasis on government investment in infrastructure most recommendations were geared toward reducing government involvement in business and encouraging outside investment.
Previous summits are credited with having influenced military ruler General Sani Abacha into carrying out a "guided deregulation" policy over the past two years.

"We are going to write a report to reflect all the recommendations, and don't be surprised if after even a week they will be prepared for implementation," Ibrahim Ida, economic advisor to the president told journalists after the meeting.
Despite the billions which Africa's most populous nation has earned through crude oil sales its economy has spiralled into ever deeper decline.
Economic policies have often stifled rather than accelerated growth as succesive military governments abruptly changed priorities.

"The time of direct government involvement in business is over and by the same token the time has passed when the private sector looked up to government for all the infrastructure needed for business," said Abacha in a speech on Wednesday.
A total of 16 separate groups debated areas of macroeconomic policy, trade and investment in both the long and short term. Next month a book will be produced containing all the recommendations.

"The military are not exactly experts in these fields, but at least if they are listening to us then some of our ideas might filter through and bear fruit," said one private sector delegate who preferred not to be named.
While economic liberalisation has swept much of the continent, Nigeria has kept more firmly to interventionist policies.
Although the government has liberalised foreign exchange, and repealed controls on external investment it has still paid little more than lip service to other areas.
Hindering a Medium Term Economic Plan, essential for talks on rescheduling a $32 billion debt, are the dual exchange rate, interest rate caps and subsidies on fuel and fertiliser.
Finance minister Anthony Ani told delegates the government was ready to abolish the dual exchange rate and fertiliser subsidy, even going as far as to suggest eventual divestment from oil production.
But at the same time he spoke of continued commitment to developing the steel industry, into which an estimated $8 billion have been ploughed without result.
Delegates, among them government ministers, said they recognised the need for revitalised privatisation or at least for competition to be permitted in key areas.
"What we see today is a serious attitude and development on key issues that is dramatically different even from previous summits," said Freddy Scott, one of the organisers.
